name: Cloud base
seoTitle: Cloud base Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Cloud base: work out cloud base altitude from the temperature and the dew point. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Cloud base calculator the temperature, the dew point and the elevation and it returns cloud base altitude. It suits a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Cloud base calculator work?
sections.html:
The Cloud base calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports cloud base altitude in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the temperature, the dew point and the elevation.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Cloud base calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Cloud base altitude=-2500 ÷ 11 × dew point + elevation + (2500 ÷ 11) × temperature
Cloud temperature=-27 ÷ 5000 × cloud base altitude + (27 ÷ 5000) × elevation + temperature

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Temperature = 10 °C, Dew point = 10 °C and Elevation = 30 m. Working through the relationship above gives Cloud base altitude = 30 m and Cloud temperature = 10 °C.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Cloud base altitude = 30 m and Cloud temperature = 10 °C should be roughly the size you expected from Temperature = 10 °C and Dew point = 10 °C.

sections.title: What does the result mean?

  • Shown in Celsius, and convertible to any of the 28 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Cloud base calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the temperature, the dew point and the elevation — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Cloud base calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The unit chips cover the units listed on the page. A historical or regional unit that is missing can still be used by converting it to a listed unit first.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

faq.q: What does the Cloud base calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns cloud base altitude, derived from the temperature, the dew point and the elevation. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Cloud base calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the temperature, the dew point and the elevation, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter temperature in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Temperature opens in Celsius and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Cloud base altitude = 30 m. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Cloud base calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
